title: Grade 4 · Equivalent fractions (4.NF.A.1)
text: Grade 4 learners explain why a fraction a/b is equal to (n x a)/(n x b) by using visual fraction models, noticing that the number and size of the parts differ even though the two fractions are the same size. The expectation is explanation with a model, not memorising a rule for multiplying numerator and denominator.

title: Grade 4 · Main idea and supporting details (RI.4.2)
text: Grade 4 learners determine the main idea of an informational text and explain how it is supported by key details, then summarise the text. The skill is distinguishing the one idea the whole text is about from the true details that back it up.

title: Common misconception: bigger denominator means bigger fraction
citation: IES Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction
text: Learners who are counting parts rather than comparing sizes often read 1/8 as larger than 1/2 because eight is larger than two. Length models such as folded paper strips of equal length make the size of one part visible, which whole-number counting strategies cannot explain away. Ask the learner to justify with the strip rather than with the numbers.

title: Common misconception: parts do not have to be equal
citation: IES Practice Guide: Developing Effective Fractions Instruction
text: A learner may shade three of five uneven pieces and call it three fifths. Folding rather than free-hand drawing forces equal parts, and comparing two strips of the same starting length keeps the whole constant, which is the other half of the idea.

title: Common misconception: the main idea is the first sentence
citation: IES Practice Guide: Improving Reading Comprehension in Kindergarten Through 3rd Grade
text: Learners often name the first sentence, or the most vivid detail, as the main idea. Asking what the whole text would lose if a sentence were removed separates the idea the text is about from a detail that supports it.

title: Offer the same idea in more than one form
text: Present the same idea physically, visually and verbally so a learner is not blocked by one channel. For a home activity that means something to hold, something to look at, and something to say out loud, rather than a worksheet that depends on reading alone.

title: Keep the working memory load low
text: Short activities with one instruction per step, and materials laid out before starting, keep attention on the idea rather than on remembering what to do next. Ten to fifteen minutes is usually enough at home.

title: Writing for families, not about them
citation: Internal guidance, aligned to IDEA progress-reporting expectations
text: Describe what the learner can already do before what comes next. Avoid grade-level comparisons, deficit words, and any mention of a disability or plan. Address the adult directly and assume ten minutes and a kitchen table, not a printer.

title: Template: hands-on model with household materials
text: Build a physical model from things already in the house, compare two versions of it, and end with the child explaining what they noticed. Steps: gather, build, compare, say it out loud. Ten to fifteen minutes. Materials must be ordinary: paper, scissors, a marker, food, coins.

title: Template: spot it in the wild
text: Find the idea somewhere in daily life and talk about it: a recipe, a road sign, a news headline, a pizza. Steps: notice one together, ask the child to find the next one, ask why it counts. No materials beyond what is already around.

title: Template: read together and say it back
text: Read a short piece aloud together, then the child says what the whole thing was about in one sentence, then finds two details that back it up. Works with a cereal box, a library book, or a short article. Ten minutes.
